title: Hotpath capture playground - notes & experiment log
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a grab-bag / playground for techniques to capture hotpath stacks and short-lived GPU/kernel activity with low overhead. It's intentionally exploratory: mix of commands, rough scripts, heuristics, and CI job sketches. The goal is a reliable, lightweight capture flow we can plug into perf CI and ad-hoc investigations without perturbing the pod latency profile too much.

Background/context:
- We already have a variety of collectors: periodic perf sampling, LTTng traces for long flows, and ad-hoc eBPF probes. Each has tradeoffs: perf is easy for user-space stacks but misses brief GPU kernels; eBPF uprobes can catch syscalls and user tracepoints but need calibration; full tracing (ftrace/lttng) is heavy.
- Recent regressions (see GH issue #312) show short 2-5ms stalls during token emission that are hard to reproduce in CI synthetic load because they happen in micro-bursts.

High-level idea:
- Combine three capture modes into a single low-impact collector: 1) low-frequency perf sampling (100-200Hz) for user stacks, 2) event-triggered eBPF micro-probes to capture kernel/GPU submit latency when certain thresholds are hit, 3) circular userspace contiguous memory ring buffer (reduced stack depth) for ultra-short spikes.
- Produce a single artifact per run: folded-stacks + flamegraph.svg + annotated trace.json (timeline with markers). CI will upload artifacts to GCS and compare flamegraph deltas with a baseline.

Quick TL;DR commands (prototype):
- perf sampling (container with root privileges / SYS_ADMIN):
  perf record -F 150 -g --call-graph dwarf -o /tmp/perf.data -- sleep 60
  perf script -i /tmp/perf.data | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > /tmp/folded.txt
  ./flamegraph.pl /tmp/folded.txt > /tmp/flame.svg

- lightweight eBPF probe (bcc / bpftrace examples):
  # bpftrace: sample nv_submit timeouts and capture user stack (uaddr stub)
  sudo bpftrace -e '
  tracepoint:gpu:gpu_submit {
    @[comm] = hist(nsecs);
  }' -o /tmp/gpu_hist.txt --duration 60

- combined wrapper (python sketch):
  - spawn perf record in background
  - start bpftrace script capturing event histograms and ring-buffer user-chunks
  - run workload (load generator)
  - after run, collect artifacts, run postproc, compress, upload

Post-processing notes:
- Use FlameGraph scripts (Brendan Gregg) for perf -> folded -> svg. Keep folded stack lines at max 200k entries, truncate deeper stacks to reduce noise.
- Annotate flamegraph with markers for token boundaries if we can inject user-level tracepoints (e.g., TRACE_TOKEN_BOUNDARY). This requires a small instrumentation shim that calls a tracepoint macro when we enqueue/dequeue tokens.
- Produce a condensed JSON timeline that lists: timestamp, pid/tid, short stack fingerprint (sha1 of top-6 frames), event-type (perf-sample|probe), and extra meta (gpu-queue-latency). This helps automated diffing.

CI integration sketch (perf-ci role):
- Add a periodic nightly Buildkite job: runtime/perf-hotpath-nightly
  - image: perf-collector:latest (with perf, bpftrace, flamegraph scripts)
  - runs canonical loadbench scenario (70/30 chat/stream mix) for 10 minutes
  - collector wrapper produces artifact: perf-flame-YYYYMMDD.tgz containing flame.svg, folded.txt, trace.json, collector.log
  - Upload to GCS path: gs://redwood-perf-artifacts/hotpath-nightly/<sha-or-date>/
  - Post step: run delta-checker against baseline. If top-10 flame entries increase > 15% p95 wall-time, fail and file a PR comment linking artifacts.

Artifact retention + baselines:
- Keep 30 days of nightly artifacts; keep tagged baselines associated with release branches (release/x.y). Baseline comparison uses top-N symbols cumulative time, and also token-boundary latency correlation where available.

Heuristics for low overhead capturing:
- perf frequency: 100-200 Hz. Higher gives better resolution but increases overhead. We must test overhead on small instances first.
- sample period length: 60s windows repeated every 10 minutes for CI to build stable estimates.
- eBPF ring-buffer sized conservatively (64KB-512KB) with an eviction policy; keep only headers for very short spikes, capture extended payload only when a threshold is exceeded.
- disable DWARF call-graph in production nightly collectors (use frame-pointer based stacks) unless we have debug symbols stored separatedly; DWARF is heavy.

Capturing GPU kernel spans (practical notes):
- NVidia: use nvtx markers from runtime to annotate enqueue points. Probe NV driver tracepoints (if allowed) for submit/complete latency. Often requires host-level driver permissions; collecting this in hosted environments may not be possible. For Dedicated/Private pools we can enable kernel-level probes.
- If driver probes not available, instrument the runtime to emit a lightweight event over UDP to the collector when submit/complete happen; collect those events alongside perf samples and correlate timestamps.

Uprobe ideas (user-space syscall and function entry/exit):
- Add temporary uprobes for critical hot functions (e.g., kvcache::lookup, token_emitter::emit_batch). Uprobes add overhead per function hit; configure to enable only when micro-regression suspected.
- For general nightly capture, rely on sampling + token boundary annotations to map stacks back to higher-level functions.

Example output interpretation heuristic (for triage):
- If folded stacks show increased area on threadpool_worker::poll_with_io, check thread-steal and blocking IO—look for thread pool saturation and slow wakeups (see SRE notes).
- If increase on memcpy/alloc/free, correlate with recent allocator changes or quantization path introducing copies.
- If short GPU submissions show longer tail, check kernel queue depths and whether kv-cache spill events align with GPU stalls.

Playground scripts (sketch files to add to runtime/tools/perf-playground):
- collect_hotpath.py  # wrapper that runs perf + bpftrace + workload, uploads artifacts
- collapse_and_annotate.sh  # runs stackcollapse, flamegraph.pl, attaches token-boundary markers
- flame_delta.py  # compares two folded.txt files and outputs the top N deltas with percentages
- trace_json_fingerprinter.py  # converts trace.json -> compact event list with stack fingerprints

Open questions / known risks:
- Hosted environments: lack of host-level privileges prevents bpftrace / perf -F on managed pods. Need an agent sidecar with elevated privileges in Dedicated only. How do we run a low-overhead collector in hosted testbeds? (Option: run in a perf-enabled bastion VM and generate load against a dedicated node.)
- Overhead: we need a small experiment matrix to quantify added p50/p95 on small, medium, large model instances for each collector config.
- Noise: sampling during GC/other tenants may pollute results. CI should pin node isolation where possible.

Immediate next steps (action items):
- [Nora] build a minimal wrapper that runs perf at 150Hz for 60s and emits folded.txt + flame.svg locally. Target: prototype by EOD 2024-11-14.
- [Miguel] prototype bpftrace event histogram for nv_submit and attempt on a dedicated dev box. Target: 2024-11-18.
- [Priya] sketch Buildkite pipeline stub and artifact upload routine; coordinate with infra for a GCS bucket. Target: 2024-11-21.
- [Ethan] run micro-overhead matrix (p50/p95 delta) with perf-only collector across 3 instance sizes and post results as a sheet. Target: 2024-11-25.

Notes and artifacts to attach later:
- baseline folded stacks (release/1.3)
- debug symbols packaging strategy (where to store .debug files, how to resolve addresses in CI)
- short script to correlate trace.json timestamps with token-boundary logs (requires synchronized clocks or monotonic counters)

Misc heuristics / tip log:
- When converting perf.data, use perf inject --timestamps if you want aligned timestamps in perf script output.
- For flame delta automation prefer a fingerprint key: (top3 frames) + library name. Avoid raw addresses in comparisons.
- Keep a small list of always-ignored frames (threadpool internals, runtime-gc, python interpreter top frames) to reduce noise in automatic alerts.

References and prior work:
- existing collectors: see perf-ci-flamegraph-tooling-wip.json (note: this doc aims to be complementary: more experimental capture techniques + CI artifactization)
- bpftrace examples: https://github.com/iovisor/bpftrace/tree/master/tests
- FlameGraph: https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph

Unresolved design questions to surface in eng sync:
- What is our tolerable overhead thresholds for nightly capture vs on-demand capture? 
- Which environments can we run privileged collectors in? (Hosted test infra? Dedicated only?)
- Do we store debug symbols in GCS or a dedicated symbol service?

If you read this and want to add a quick experiment: drop a short bash script or a Buildkite step suggestion in the comments below. I'll keep iterating and will move stable parts into runtime/tools/perf-playground and a Buildkite job once we have the overhead matrix.
